item.title: What if the Most Essential Tool in Therapy Is You?
item.description:
Therapy

What if the Most Essential Tool in Therapy Is You?

Actors can teach therapists and clients about what matters most in psychotherapy.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Research consistently shows that the psychotherapeutic relationship matters more than a particular technique.
  • How therapists show up—their presence, voice, body, and responsiveness—is as important as interventions.
  • Actors can show therapists how to be present, adapt, and invite clients into connection and possibility.
Niecy Nash as Dr. Jamie Ryan in "Never Have I Ever"
Source: Courtesy of Netflix

Psychotherapy research is both illuminating and humbling. After a century of developing theories, modalities, evidence-based treatments, and “best practices,” we keep returning to the same fact:

The effectiveness of therapy depends not on any particular technique, but on the individual therapist, the individual client, and “the unique patterns of interaction that develop between them” (Shedler, 2012).

While a wide range of therapy models have proven to be helpful for specific people at specific times, studies show that it doesn’t necessarily matter whether a therapist practices ACT, CBT, DBT, EFT, EMDR, or psychoanalysis. What matters is how the two people in the room engage one another (Shedler, 2012; Stendi & Matos, 2023; Cruwys et al., 2023).

A recent New York Times article about our endless search for a one-size-fits-all psychotherapy approach emphasizes this point. The author, Daniel Duane, brilliantly provides thorough, cogent, and accessible context for how the therapy conversation has evolved and expanded over the years, and what remains consistent: the primary importance of the therapeutic relationship (Duane, 2026).

Duane concludes by introducing predictive processing, a neuroscience-based theory that explains why clients tend to protect themselves from vulnerability and change, and how the therapist/client relationship has the potential to free people from these patterns, no matter what technique is used (Corlett et al., 2020).

Predictive processing certainly helps explain why the unique relationship is in fact what matters most in psychotherapy. And yet, despite his attempt to do the opposite, Duane can’t entirely resist the very quest for a unifying psychotherapy theory that it intends to critique.

Is there truly a way out of this dilemma?

I believe there is.

Rather than attempting to find one convincingly rigorous approach to therapy, what if we simply let the research speak for itself?

What if we accepted that what therapists and researchers all tend to agree on actually matters—that how a therapist engages a particular client matters more than which intervention they use? Even iconic CBT therapist Judith Beck believes the most effective way to establish meaningful connections with clients, beyond behavioral technique, is through "empathic statements, choice of words, tone of voice, facial expressions and body language” (Beck, 2011).

If we begin with this premise, then the next question becomes, How do we help therapists maximize the use of their most essential instrument: themselves?

The Therapist as Instrument

Therapists receive endless training on what to do in session. We constantly learn “cutting-edge” ways to identify symptoms, ask questions, challenge distorted thinking, regulate affect, interpret, reflect, validate, guide, and perform interventions toward optimal mental health.

But how therapists do all of this is rarely, if ever, discussed.

For instance: How does a therapist show up on a given day, with enough awareness of what is happening in their mind and body to deliver their interventions with clear intentions, even when they’re just listening? How do our reactions, responses, questions, and clinical choices show up in our faces, breathing, voices, and bodies? What are we actually doing in the room, moment-to-moment, as we exchange attention with our “scene partners” (as I like to refer to my clients), as opposed to what we think we’re doing?

This is where my background as both a psychotherapist and a trained actor has profoundly shaped my clinical work.

Actors don’t simply memorize text and actions, and execute them with certainty and precision. They listen to each individual scene partner and the circumstances of each scene (O'Connell, 2023), remain aware of their intentions and responses, and adapt in real time as their scene partner makes a move of their own. Their task is to remain present and alive enough to keep the scene open to possibility.

This is also true for psychotherapy.

Invitation vs. Intervention: The Client Is Not a Problem to Solve

One of the pitfalls of searching for the “perfect" therapy tool is that we begin to view challenging moments in therapy as failures of technique.

  • What intervention should I use?

  • What certification did I fail to get?

  • Why isn't this working?!

Whereas, we could instead ask much more salient and productive questions at these times:

  • What is happening between us right now?

  • What is keeping us stuck in a mode of self-protection?

And most importantly:

  • How can I make an invitation to my scene partner to participate in this process with a sense of connection and possibility?

Robin Weigert as Dr. Amanda Reisman in "Big Little Lies," season 2.
Source: Courtesy of HBO

Like acting scene partners, clients don’t simply bring symptoms into the room to be solved. They bring individual, complex, and nuanced ways of relating, protecting themselves, and reaching toward the person across from them, trying to discover whether or not it’s safe enough to be present with them.

And therapists do the same thing.

If we acknowledge this is happening between every therapeutic couple, our goal becomes less about finding the “best” intervention and more about discovering the most effective invitation for each scene partner to enter the playing space with us. Then we can draw upon whatever tools we’ve learned not as prescriptions for what will “fix a problem,” but as resources to help us make that invitation.

We can look to actors for practical ways to prepare our instruments for the uncertainty of each “scene.” Take actor Robin Weigert’s wonderful paper, "Listening into Being," in Psychoanalytic Inquiry as one example. (Weigert has also played therapists on screen, including in the HBO series Big Little Lies.)

We can also make use of decades of illuminating research from psychologist/psychoanalyst Beatrice Beebe. Dr. Beebe has studied nonverbal communication between the “scene partners” of parent and infant, as well as between therapist and client, showing us how to use our instruments to make meaningful invitations to other people (Sandberg & Beebe, 2020).

Case Illustration

I will leave you with an evocative anecdote as you consider my invitation here.

Legendary actress Olympia Dukakis often told a story about working with her husband on a production of Long Day’s Journey Into Night. They had performed the play twice before, thinking they’d mastered it. “You’d think, what is there to unearth?” she initially observed.

But during one rehearsal, she became blocked. She complained to the director (who was her brother) that she did not know what to do since her husband was not making the right choices (not deploying “best practices,” if you will); thus, she could not do the scene right. Her brother replied that he too was at a loss, not knowing how to help when she clearly “wanted to control the stage.”

Hard as this was to hear, Olympia allowed herself to say “Yes” to her husband’s choices, risked losing her expectations (her masterful “treatment plan”), and surrendered to the process. She later said, “What I had rejected was exactly what I needed to see. I had to stop trying to win. I had to start playing again."

Being open to her husband’s invitation to find potential in the play together helped Olympia discover living, breathing possibility in a story she had initially decided was old hat (O'Connell, 2019).

Now let’s go find that potential in the therapy room.

item.title: When Being the Best Is Still Not Enough
item.description:
Sport and Competition

When Being the Best Is Still Not Enough

Early experiences can shape the physiology driving our pursuit of greatness.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Achievement may not resolve the deeper feeling that we are not enough.
  • Early experiences can shape the physiology beneath our hunger, drive, and relentless commitment to achieve.
  • Attuning to our physiology can help shift our relationship with performance and achievement.
Source: LUSAIL, LOSAIL / Shutterstock

Novak Djokovic has achieved virtually everything possible in professional tennis. He is widely considered one of the greatest, if not the greatest, players of all time. Yet in the newly released documentary Novak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter, he reflects on something deeply vulnerable that may be familiar to all of us: “The feeling of not good enough has been with me for a very long time. It’s still with me.”

There is something both striking and human about hearing those words from such an accomplished icon who often portrays so much bravado and confidence on his stage.

We live within a culture that repeatedly encourages us to compete, compare, perform, achieve, and prove ourselves. Today’s performance is no longer good enough tomorrow. We tackle one goal, and we immediately begin pursuing the next. We become better than before, but we quickly compare ourselves to someone else or to another standard we have yet to meet.

Achievement can become an attempt to secure something deeper that our biology is seeking: safety, resources, approval, belonging, or a sense that we are finally good enough.

Djokovic’s honest reflection is a powerful reminder that achievement, even at the highest level, does not necessarily erase the deeper physiological imprint of never feeling like we are enough.

In the documentary, Djokovic describes what can happen when our own achievements continually raise the bar for what is considered enough. He calls it the “curse of achieving every possible achievement,” because anything less can begin to feel not good enough. Elsewhere, he acknowledges, “I cannot say I feel content with what I have and who I am.”

When this happens, performance becomes more than something we do. It becomes something we depend upon to establish who we are and whether we are enough. Importantly, this shift is not necessarily the result of a conscious decision made by Djokovic, or any of us. It can become embodied within our physiology itself. Beneath his record-setting Grand Slam titles, Djokovic's relationship with the tennis court and with achievement may have been shaped, in part, by a physiological imprint formed through his early experiences in childhood.

When he was 12 years old, his father revealed to his entire family how little money they had left, and how much of it was going toward supporting Novak’s development. It was a tremendous sacrifice and gamble that the entire family understood. For Djokovic, that decision appears to have carried a very powerful and relentless pressure to perform. He remembers, “I had to become more serious, more stern, more stable, more of a man rather than a boy.”

Whatever meaning tennis held for Djokovic before that moment, something had changed. Succeeding became intertwined with responsibility, family resources, sacrifice, and the knowledge that the people he cared about most were depending upon him. Imagine how that might feel at only 12 years old.

Recognizing this does not mean we have to stop competing, pursuing goals and dreams, working hard, or committing ourselves to what matters to us. But perhaps we can develop a different relationship with achievement and become more attuned to the physiology accompanying what motivates us.

We can’t know exactly what continues to drive Djokovic today, but his own reflections give us a useful lens through which to consider what may sit beneath his relentless pursuit of more.

So when I see Djokovic still competing today, pressing hard, sacrificing whatever it takes, and even struggling physically at times, I don’t see someone who simply believes he can still compete with the best, or someone who doesn’t know when to stop. I see that same little boy, still shaped and fueled by the physiological imprint of what winning has always meant.

And when I think back to Djokovic breaking down in tears, running into the stands, and collapsing into his mother’s arms after finally winning Olympic gold, I see more than an athlete celebrating the achievement he wanted most, and one that had eluded him. I see the little boy who had taken on so much responsibility at such a young age, almost as if he were saying, "Mom, I did it. I didn’t let you or the family down."
